function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

function.name: write_markdown_tool
function.description: Writes the provided content to a Markdown (.md) file on the disk. This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: write_html_tool
function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance with a GPU (the closest available to an RTX A6000) and Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.  
It includes:

* **Prerequisites** – what you need to enable and configure beforehand.  
* **gcloud CLI command** – the simplest way to launch the instance.  
* **REST API (curl) call** – if you prefer to use the raw Compute Engine API.  
* **Notes** – about GPU availability, billing, and driver installation.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

| Step | What to do | Why |
|------|------------|-----|
| 1 | **Enable the Compute Engine API** | Required for all Compute Engine operations. |
| 2 | **Enable the Cloud Resource Manager API** | Needed for project‑level operations. |
| 3 | **Create a service account** (or use your own user account) | Needed for authentication and IAM permissions. |
| 4 | **Grant the service account the “Compute Admin” role** (`roles/compute.admin`) | Allows it to create instances. |
| 5 | **Add the “Cloud Platform” scope** (`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform`) | Gives full access to GCP resources. |
| 6 | **Set up billing** for the project | GPU instances incur charges. |
| 7 | **Choose a zone that supports GPUs** | Not all zones have GPU hardware. |
| 8 | **Check GPU availability** | Use `gcloud compute accelerator-types list` to confirm the GPU type. |

> **GPU note** – Google Cloud does not currently offer an NVIDIA RTX A6000.  
> The closest equivalent is the **NVIDIA Tesla A100** (`nvidia-tesla-a100`).  
> If you absolutely need an RTX A6000, you would have to use a different provider (e.g., AWS, Azure) or a custom‑hardware VM.

---

## 2. gcloud CLI Command

```bash
# Variables (replace with your own values)
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"                     # choose a zone that supports GPUs
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-demo"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8"             # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM
GPU_TYPE="nvidia-tesla-a100"             # closest to RTX A6000
GPU_COUNT=1
DISK_SIZE_GB=100
DISK_TYPE="pd-ssd"
SERVICE_ACCOUNT="my-sa@${PROJECT_ID}.iam.gserviceaccount.com"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "${INSTANCE_NAME}" \
  --project="${PROJECT_ID}" \
  --zone="${ZONE}" \
  --machine-type="${MACHINE_TYPE}" \
  --accelerator=type=${GPU_TYPE},count=${GPU_COUNT} \
  --image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts \
  --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
  --boot-disk-size=${DISK_SIZE_GB}GB \
  --boot-disk-type=${DISK_TYPE} \
  --service-account="${SERVICE_ACCOUNT}" \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh
```

### `startup.sh` (optional)

If you want the GPU drivers installed automatically on boot, create a file named `startup.sh` in the same directory:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Update package lists
apt-get update

# Install NVIDIA driver (example: 525.x)
apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-525

# Verify installation
nvidia-smi
```

Make sure the script is executable:

```bash
chmod +x startup.sh
```

---

## 3. REST API (curl) Call

If you prefer to use the raw Compute Engine API, the following `curl` command does the same thing.  
Replace the placeholder values (`{PROJECT_ID}`, `{ZONE}`, etc.) with your actual data.

```bash
# Get an access token (requires gcloud SDK)
ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)

# JSON payload
read -r -d '' INSTANCE_JSON <<EOF
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-demo",
  "machineType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/${ZONE}/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/${ZONE}/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/${ZONE}/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        {
          "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT",
          "name": "External NAT"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "${SERVICE_ACCOUNT}",
      "scopes": [
        "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\\napt-get update\\napt-get install -y nvidia-driver-525\\nnvidia-smi"
      }
    ]
  }
}
EOF

# Make the API call
curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "${INSTANCE_JSON}" \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/${ZONE}/instances"
```

> **Tip** – If you’re running this from a machine that doesn’t have the `gcloud` SDK, you can obtain an OAuth 2.0 token via the Google Cloud Console or by using a service account key file.

---

## 4. After Creation

1. **Verify the instance**  
   ```bash
   gcloud compute instances describe rtx-a6000-demo --zone=${ZONE}
   ```
2. **SSH into the instance**  
   ```bash
   gcloud compute ssh rtx-a6000-demo --zone=${ZONE}
   ```
3. **Check GPU status**  
   ```bash
   nvidia-smi
   ```
   You should see the NVIDIA A100 GPU listed.

---

## 5. Billing & Cost

| Item | Approximate Cost (USD per hour) |
|------|---------------------------------|
| n1-standard-8 (8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM) | ~0.40 |
| NVIDIA Tesla A100 (1 GPU) | ~2.50 |
| SSD boot disk (100 GB) | ~0.10 |
| **Total** | ~3.00 |

> Costs vary by region and by whether you use preemptible instances.  
> Always check the [Google Cloud Pricing Calculator](https://cloud.google.com/products/calculator) for the latest numbers.

---

## 6. Summary

* **Use the `gcloud` CLI** for quick, interactive instance creation.  
* **Use the REST API** if you need programmatic control or integration with other systems.  
* **Replace the GPU type** with `nvidia-tesla-a100` (closest to RTX A6000).  
* **Install drivers** via a startup script or manually after SSH.  

Happy computing!
